\chapter{Five Words for Weighing One Thing Against Another}
\label{ch:barato-y-caro}
\hlchaptermodality{397}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say barato, caro, gratis, mayor and menor, and say how one thing compares with another.}

Complete ES-C397-menor: weigh one thing against another, and say why.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[barato]{barato — a price that started out as a shady deal}

\label{lesson:ES-C397-barato}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to work, to run}, then \emph{to repair}. (\emph{Funcionar}; \emph{reparar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el precio — what this word is about.
  \item el dinero — what you hand over.
  \item comprar — what you are doing when the price matters.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ba-RA-to}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{r} is one quick tap, and the \emph{b} between two vowels is soft — lips close only halfway. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{barato} — \textquotedblleft{}cheap.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it sits an old verb, \textbf{baratar}, \textquotedblleft{}to trade, to haggle, to do a deal.\textquotedblright{} The Academy's dictionary gives that verb four words: \emph{de origen incierto} — of uncertain origin. Corominas adds what can be added and no more: the verb turns up across Spanish, French and Italian alike, and is \emph{probably pre-Roman, and perhaps Celtic.} That is where the trail stops, and this lesson stops there too.

What is \emph{not} uncertain is the direction the meaning came from. Corominas is explicit that \emph{barato} in the sense \textquotedblleft{}low-priced\textquotedblright{} was born attached to the idea of a \textbf{shady bargain} — cheap because of the circumstances of the deal, not because of anything measurable about the thing. The price was a comment on the dealing.

English has a word from the same guess, reached from the same direction: \textbf{barter}. Old French \emph{barater} meant \textquotedblleft{}to barter, to cheat, to haggle,\textquotedblright{} and the dictionaries that hunt its origin land on the same Celtic hypothesis Corominas lands on. So \emph{barato} and \emph{barter} are relatives at the level of the family — not a line anyone has traced end to end, which is why this says \emph{family} and not \emph{ancestor}.

One story you will meet and should not repeat: that \emph{barato} comes from Greek \emph{prattein}, \textquotedblleft{}to do business,\textquotedblright{} carried by Greek merchants. Corominas rejects it on the sounds alone, and there were no Greek merchants in medieval Spain to carry it. It is tidy, it is everywhere, and it is not true.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un hotel barato} — a cheap hotel;
  \item \emph{muy barato} — very cheap.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now price a thing low: \emph{barato}. And you have met a word whose origin the best dictionary in the language declines to give — which is itself worth seeing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{barato}
  \item \emph{un hotel barato}
  \item \emph{muy barato}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{baratar} mean? (\emph{To trade, to haggle}.) And what does the dictionary say about where it came from? (\emph{That it is uncertain} — probably pre-Roman, perhaps Celtic.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[caro]{caro — the word English keeps saying as \textquotedblleft{}dear\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C397-caro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to repair}, then \emph{cheap}. (\emph{Reparar}; \emph{barato}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item barato — the other end of the same scale.
  \item la cara — a different word you already own. Hold on to it.
  \item cero — and this one too.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CA-ro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{r} is one tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{caro} — \textquotedblleft{}expensive.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{cārus} meant \emph{beloved} — and it also meant \emph{costly}. Both, from the start. Nothing had to move.

English does the same thing today and nobody notices. \emph{My dear friend.} \emph{That coat is a bit dear.} One word, both jobs, exactly as in Spanish — and this is a coincidence of habit, not of ancestry: English \emph{dear} is a Germanic word and is not related to \emph{cārus} at all. Spanish keeps both jobs too, and \emph{caro amigo} is still readable, though it now sounds bookish.

Three ordinary English words \emph{are} from \emph{cārus}, all of them arriving through Romance:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{charity} — from \emph{cāritās}, \textquotedblleft{}costliness, esteem, affection\textquotedblright{};
  \item \textbf{cherish} — from Old French \emph{chierir};
  \item \textbf{caress} — through Italian \emph{carezza}, whose Spanish sibling is \emph{caricia}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Now the two words that look like this one and are not this one.}

\emph{La cara} is a face. \emph{Cara} is also what \emph{caro} becomes before a feminine noun. So the same four letters do two unrelated jobs, and what tells you which is what comes \textbf{before} it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cara} — the face; a noun with \emph{la} in front;
  \item \emph{una casa cara} — an expensive house; \emph{cara} sitting after the thing it describes.
\end{itemize}

And \emph{cero} is not this word either. \emph{Cero} is the number nought. One vowel apart, and it is the only vowel doing any work:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{caro} — expensive;
  \item \emph{cero} — zero.
\end{itemize}

Say the pair aloud twice and the \emph{a} stops being optional.

Finally, one trap from the dictionary shelf. Latin has a second \emph{caro} — \emph{caro, carnis}, \textquotedblleft{}flesh\textquotedblright{} — which gives Spanish \emph{carne} and English \emph{carnival}. Same spelling in an index, different word entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now price a thing high: \emph{caro}. And you can keep \emph{caro}, \emph{cara} and \emph{cero} apart by what stands in front of them and by one vowel.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{caro}
  \item \emph{una casa cara}
  \item \emph{barato, caro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two things did Latin \emph{cārus} mean at once? (\emph{Beloved}, and \emph{costly}.) In \emph{la cara}, what tells you this is a face and not a price? (\emph{La} — it is a noun here.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gratis]{gratis — a Latin word that never unpacked}

\label{lesson:ES-C397-gratis}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{cheap}, then \emph{expensive}. (\emph{Barato}; \emph{caro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item gracias — the word this one is built out of.
  \item el precio — what \emph{gratis} says there isn't one of.
  \item pagar — what you do not do.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{GRA-tis}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{g} is hard, the \emph{r} is one tap, and the final \emph{s} is clear. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gratis} — \textquotedblleft{}free of charge.\textquotedblright{}

You already own the root. \emph{Gracias} is \textbf{grātia}, \textquotedblleft{}favour, thanks.\textquotedblright{} And \emph{gratis} is the same noun in a case form — Latin \textbf{grātiīs}, squeezed down to \textbf{grātīs} — which the Romans used to mean \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}for thanks.\textquotedblright{}}

That is the whole idea. You are not paying money for it. You are paying in gratitude.

Look at what that history left behind. \emph{Barato} and \emph{caro} bend to fit the noun they sit beside:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un hotel barato}, \emph{una casa cara};
\end{itemize}

and \emph{gratis} does not:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un café \textbf{gratis}}, \emph{una entrada \textbf{gratis}}.
\end{itemize}

It arrived in Spanish as a finished Latin word rather than growing up inside the language, so it never learned the endings. The same fossil is sitting in English, which borrowed \emph{gratis} in the 1400s and left it alone in exactly the same way.

The rest of the family is large and mostly English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{grace}, \textbf{gracious}, \textbf{grateful}, \textbf{gratitude};
  \item \textbf{gratuity} — a tip, money given for thanks;
  \item \textbf{gratuitous} — which still does both jobs, meaning \emph{free of charge} and also \emph{uncalled-for}, because both are \textquotedblleft{}given for nothing.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{(Grammarians file} grātiīs \emph{as dative-or-ablative, since Latin ran the two together in the plural; it is read as ablative here.)}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing costs nothing: \emph{gratis}. And you can hear it as \emph{gracias} wearing a Latin ending — which is why it never changes shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gratis}
  \item \emph{un café gratis}
  \item \emph{una entrada gratis}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{gratis} literally say you are paying with? (\emph{Thanks} — it is \emph{gracias} in a Latin case form.) So why is there no \emph{gratisa}? (It came in as a finished Latin word and never took Spanish endings.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mayor]{mayor — the greater one, and the man at the town hall}

\label{lesson:ES-C397-mayor}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{expensive}, then \emph{free of charge}. (\emph{Caro}; \emph{gratis}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item grande — the plain word this one is the step above.
  \item el hermano, la hermana — who you will use it about.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-YOR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{y} is the same sound Spanish writes with \emph{ll}, and the final \emph{r} is one tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mayor} — \textquotedblleft{}bigger,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}older.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{maior} is the comparative of \textbf{magnus}, \textquotedblleft{}great.\textquotedblright{} Not \emph{bigger} as a separate word — \emph{great}, with the comparison built in. \emph{Greater.}

Spanish runs it two ways, and the exam will want both:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mi hermano \textbf{mayor}} — my \textbf{older} brother;
  \item \emph{personas \textbf{mayores}} — \textbf{older} people;
  \item \emph{la plaza \textbf{mayor}} — the \textbf{main} square, the greater one.
\end{itemize}

English carries the same Latin word twice. \textbf{Major} is the obvious one. The other is \textbf{mayor} — the head of a town, who is, quite literally, \emph{the greater man}. Beside them sit \textbf{majority}, \textbf{majesty}, and the wider \emph{magnus} family: \textbf{magnify}, \textbf{magnificent}, \textbf{maximum}.

\textbf{And here is the part worth keeping.} English put that word to work at the town hall. Spanish did not. The Spanish official is \textbf{el alcalde} — from Arabic \emph{al-qāḍī}, \textquotedblleft{}the judge.\textquotedblright{} Two languages inherited one Latin word, and only one of them handed it the job.

One story to leave alone: that the month \textbf{mayo} is \emph{maior} as well, named for the elders. Dictionaries derive \emph{Maius} from the goddess \textbf{Maia}, and the elders-and-youngers tale is an old guess repeated ever since. \emph{Mayo} and \emph{mayor} are not the same word, whatever the four shared letters suggest.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing is bigger, or a person older: \emph{mayor}. And you know one job English gives it that Spanish gives to an Arabic word instead.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mayor}
  \item \emph{mi hermano mayor}
  \item \emph{personas mayores}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Mayor} is the comparative of which Latin word? (\emph{Magnus}, \textquotedblleft{}great\textquotedblright{} — so it means \emph{greater}.) What does Spanish call the mayor of a town, and where is that word from? (\emph{El alcalde}, from Arabic \emph{al-qāḍī}, \textquotedblleft{}the judge.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[menor]{menor — and the minister Latin built to face the master}

\label{lesson:ES-C397-menor}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{free of charge}, then \emph{bigger, older}. (\emph{Gratis}; \emph{mayor}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mayor — the one this answers.
  \item pequeño — the plain word it steps above.
  \item menos — you own this already. Keep it close; it is not this word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{me-NOR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The final \emph{r} is one tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{menor} — \textquotedblleft{}smaller,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}younger.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{minor} is the partner of \textbf{minus}, which you already have. \emph{Minus} is the neuter; \emph{minor} is the one you use of people and things.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mi hermana \textbf{menor}} — my \textbf{younger} sister;
  \item \emph{\textbf{menor} de edad} — under age, a minor.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Now hold it against the word you already own.} \emph{Menos} and \emph{menor} are one letter apart at the end, and that letter is the whole difference:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{menos}} — \emph{less}, the amount. \emph{Menos dinero.}
  \item \emph{\textbf{menor}} — \emph{smaller, younger}, said of a thing or a person. \emph{Mi hermana menor.}
\end{itemize}

Same root, two jobs. Say them as a pair — \emph{menos, menor} — and the ending starts doing the work.

Now the shape of the pair with \emph{mayor}. \emph{Menor} serves as the step above \emph{pequeño}, and \emph{mayor} as the step above \emph{grande} — but neither is built from the word it serves. Latin took them from somewhere else entirely, the way English reaches for \emph{better} instead of \emph{gooder}.

And Latin did something deliberate with this root. \textbf{Minister} is \textbf{minus} plus the ending \emph{-ter} — and it was made that way \emph{to stand opposite} \textbf{magister}, which is \textbf{magis} (\textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}) plus the same \emph{-ter}. The lesser one and the greater one, built as a matched pair. English holds both: \textbf{minister} and \textbf{master}.

The rest of the family is everywhere once you look: \textbf{minus}, \textbf{minute} (both the small kind and the sixty-second kind), \textbf{diminish}, \textbf{minimum}, \textbf{mince}, and \textbf{menu} — a \emph{small} list.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing is smaller, or a person younger: \emph{menor}. You have five words for weighing one thing against another — \emph{barato}, \emph{caro}, \emph{gratis}, \emph{mayor}, \emph{menor} — and you can keep \emph{menor} apart from \emph{menos} by its last letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{menor}
  \item \emph{mi hermana menor}
  \item \emph{menos, menor}
  \item \emph{barato, caro, gratis, mayor, menor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{menos} and \emph{menor} would you use for \emph{my younger sister}? (\emph{Menor} — \emph{mi hermana menor}.) And which two English words did Latin build as a deliberate pair from \emph{minus} and \emph{magis}? (\emph{Minister} and \emph{master}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
